title: Isomorphism dichotomy for finitely forbidden hereditary classes
formal: For every finite family \(\mathcal F\) of finite graphs, is graph isomorphism restricted to graphs containing no induced copy of a member of \(\mathcal F\) either solvable in deterministic polynomial time or complete for general graph isomorphism under polynomial-time many-one reductions?

why: A finite list of forbidden induced patterns is a simple and widely used graph-class description. The conjecture asks whether such finite structural restrictions always make symmetry testing tractable or retain the full difficulty of unrestricted graph isomorphism.
status_note: Conjecture 1 is explicit in the 2015 source. Its quantifiers and partial theorem were checked on 13 September 2026; the limited later-work check supplied no verified resolution for arbitrary finite forbidden families. Status is source_open.

progress.text: The paper states the finite-family dichotomy as Conjecture 1 and establishes the polynomial-time versus isomorphism-complete alternatives for all but finitely many two-forbidden-pattern cases.

category_assignment.reason: Computational complexity of isomorphism on hereditary graph classes.

importance.reason: A general finite-description dichotomy for hereditary isomorphism, asking whether finite induced obstructions eliminate intermediate complexity.

sentences: Hereditary graph classes can be specified by finitely many forbidden induced subgraphs.
The question asks whether graph isomorphism on such a class can have complexity intermediate between polynomial time and general graph-isomorphism completeness.
The source establishes broad classifications and resolves most two-forbidden-pattern cases.
Results for forbidden ordinary subgraphs do not immediately extend to induced exclusions.
The project seeks a dichotomy explaining whether a finite structural prohibition always makes isomorphism substantially easier or leaves its full general difficulty intact.

definitions: All graphs are finite, undirected and simple, with binary adjacency-matrix encodings. The finite forbidden family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed, not part of the input. Let \(\mathcal C_{\mathcal F}\) contain every graph with no induced subgraph isomorphic to a member of \(\mathcal F\). Its isomorphism task receives two members \(G_1,G_2\) and asks whether there is a vertex bijection preserving adjacency and nonadjacency. Polynomial time means worst-case deterministic bit time bounded by a polynomial in their combined encoding length; the machine and polynomial may depend on \(\mathcal F\). Graph-isomorphism completeness means that there is a deterministic polynomial-time map from any pair of arbitrary simple graphs to a pair in \(\mathcal C_{\mathcal F}\), preserving the YES/NO isomorphism answer. The reverse reduction is the identity. Outputs of the hardness reduction must satisfy the class promise on both YES and NO inputs. Class membership can be checked in polynomial time for fixed finite \(\mathcal F\), so a total-language formulation may reject encodings outside the class. No algorithm deciding which side applies from an input description of \(\mathcal F\) is required. The alternatives need not be disjoint if general graph isomorphism is in P; the conjecture asserts their union covers every finite forbidden family.

context_blocks.text: Schweitzer’s Conjecture 1 asks for a polynomial-time versus general-isomorphism-complete dichotomy for finitely forbidden hereditary classes. Finiteness of the forbidden induced family is essential: the discussion distinguishes conditional intermediate examples requiring infinite descriptions.

The source obtains the dichotomy for all but finitely many two-forbidden-graph cases. A classification by forbidden ordinary subgraphs also does not settle the conjecture, because induced exclusions allow a broader range of structural behavior.

answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated universal dichotomy, or exhibit a fixed finite forbidden family and prove that its restricted isomorphism problem has neither property. A complete proof may use a mathematically specified classification without an effective classifier for forbidden families. A two-pattern theorem alone, a result for ordinary subgraph exclusion, or NP-hardness terminology without the required graph-isomorphism reductions does not settle the target.

notes: Recovered the exact finite-family quantifier and Conjecture 1, rather than conflating it with the paper’s almost-complete two-pattern theorem.
Defined promise-preserving many-one graph-isomorphism completeness and fixed-family polynomial time.
Did not require an effective meta-classifier or assume the two alternatives are disjoint when general graph isomorphism could be in P.
